chapter_theme: Natrinai 201 to 220: hill courtships pressed toward marriage by millet harvests, a mother's look and a madal the children play at; shore girls who lament nightfall or refuse to blame the man they chose; paalai partings for wealth weighed against a wife's beauty and mocked by the promised rain; and marutham rebukes that define true wealth as fear of a dependant's distress.

201.reading: The man answers the companion who told him the hill hunter's young daughter is too closely guarded, too young and too unwilling to be thought of: like the image on Kolli's western hill that the god guards, which no wind, lashing rain, thunder or heaving earth can move, she will not leave his heart.
201.nuance: The companion's four objections (hard to win, guarded, deaf to words, young) are met by five assaults on the image (wind, rain, thunder, many harms, the earth rising), so the reply outnumbers the rebuke; and the guarded girl is answered by a guarded image, the god's keeping set against her father's.

colophon.thurai: கழறிய பாங்கற்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a hill girl held fast in the lover's heart during secret love

comparisons.vehicle: திரு நல உருவின் மாயா இயற்கைப் பாவையின்
comparisons.tenor: the girl, fixed in his heart

202.reading: Eloping with the girl, the man bids her look at the great hill's rifts, where a tusker whose tusk reddened fighting a tiger breaks a thick tree and feeds his cow and calf golden mouthfuls of vengai, and at the forest decked with kongam flowers like the long rows of lamps lit in the holy month of the six stars.
202.nuance: The festival of the Karthigai month is the girl's home festival, so the hero dresses the strange forest in the lights she has just left; நுந்தை in line 8 (your father) is hard to place, and may tie the lamps to her father's town.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the lover leading the girl through the forest in elopement

comparisons.tenor: the vengai flowers fed to the cow

comparisons.vehicle: அறம் செய் திங்கள் செல் சுடர் நெடுங் கொடி
comparisons.tenor: the kongam in flower across the forest

iraicchi.act: the tusker embraces his young cow and calf and feeds them golden mouthfuls of vengai
iraicchi.sense: the man leading her away from her kin will feed and shelter her on the road as the tusker does his mate

203.reading: With the man listening, the friend says that in the fragrant shore grove, where screwpine flowers like drawn-out conch burst their pollen under the waves and wipe the fish smell from the hamlet's street, their bond was formed, and he, not thinking a day apart unbearable, has let his swift chariot stop coming, a fault of his own, while this noisy town has fallen into distress.
203.nuance: The screwpine's scent that overcomes the street's fish smell is a near miss for ullurai (the love whose fragrance escapes into the town as talk): only one pair is clear, so it stays scene; the closing 'this clamorous town' turns the gossip itself into the sufferer.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாக தோழி சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: screwpine, shore grove and fishing hamlet, with the friend pressing for marriage

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is not named; the poem speaks of 'our bond' to the girl

204.reading: The man who has followed the girl tells his heart, with the friend listening, how he asked whether he should come at dusk to her father's millet field wearing a leaf skirt or bathe with her on the slope of their meeting, begging a word to slake his heart; she answered by naming sweetly the place of tryst, and went off changed, like a young doe parted from its stag, to the bamboo-high village, and his heart, sent after her, will not let her go.
204.nuance: He offers to come in a leaf skirt (தழை), the girl's own dress, so the lover proposes to pass unseen as one of the millet guards; and the heart he 'sent' with her is the subject of the last line, as if the heart, not he, had refused to return.

colophon.thurai: பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் ஆற்றானாய் தோழி கேட்பத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, the hill slope and the hill girl naming a tryst

comparisons.tenor: the girl turning away from him

205.reading: The man tells his heart, which counts as nothing the forest by the waterfall slopes where the aali drags off the white-tusked bull elephant that killed a striped tiger, that if he leaves for wealth with her here, her dark beauty, like the fine colour of tender mango and thorny eengai shoots in the garden after heavy rain, will be gone from this very day.
205.nuance: The forest's chain of killing (tiger by elephant, elephant by aali) measures danger to the traveller; the beauty at home is measured by tender rain-washed shoots, so the poem sets the strongest beast against the most perishable leaf, and the leaf wins: he stays.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லி செலவு அழுங்கியது தோழி செலவு அழுங்கச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: a parting for wealth across a hard forest, weighed and put off

206.reading: The friend, with the man listening, says that father came saying the milky millet ears are bending and red-beaked parrots gather on the rocks, so beat the clapper and string the sling; and mother, saying 'now may the vengai of the good day flower', looked at her face: does she mean to let them go out or to shut them in, and has she learned of their bond with the man of the stony land?
206.nuance: The vengai's flowering marks the season of weddings, so the mother's wish is ambiguous on purpose: a wedding with a stranger or a suspicion of the lover; the friend's 'I do not know' is the pressure on the listening man.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarding, parrots and the vengai, in secret love near discovery

207.reading: Telling the foster mother the truth when strangers seek the girl, the friend says a tall chariot keeps coming noisily to the fishers' hamlet of thatched huts among the backwaters, crossing dunes like hills, and asks whether its rider will turn back; yet in a night gathering of young and old, the girl of the old shark-scarred fishermen has been given to the murderous young men who go to sea with net and line.
207.nuance: The chariot is the lover's and marks a man not of the fishers; the friend sets it against the kin's choice of sea-going youths, so the revelation is made by contrast, without naming him; who the 'fierce youths' are (the strangers' party or the girl's own kin) is not certain.

colophon.thurai: நொதுமலர் வரைவுழி தோழி செவிலிக்கு அறத்தொடு நின்றது

thinai_evidence.note: backwaters, fishermen and their nets

208.reading: The friend asks the weeping girl why she wilts, her bangles loosening and tears clear as stream water wetting her breasts: their lover will not go, and if he goes he cannot bear the pain; he deserves trust, loves deeply and grieves more than they, and will come back even with his wealth unwon; besides, this great rain's voice sounds as if it were seeking out those parted from sweet partners to bring them home.
208.nuance: The friend reasons in steps (he won't go; if he goes he'll suffer; if he suffers he'll return), then gives the clinching proof to the rain, which she makes a fetcher of the parted.

colophon.thurai: செலவுற்றாரது குறிப்பு அறிந்து ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் உரைப்ப தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a feared parting for wealth

209.reading: Refused, the man tells his heart that the girl in the millet field, where hill farmers sowed a few seeds widely on a cleared slope after rain and reaped plenty, has a sweet lisping voice that even the parrots know; when it reaches him his sorrow ends, and if it stays away it will take his life and everything with it.
209.nuance: The few seeds that yield a heavy crop sit beside the friend's small favour he begs for (the colophon says the friend hears and grants the suit); one pair only, so a near miss for ullurai, left as scene. The parrots 'know' her voice because they hear her scare them all day.

colophon.thurai: குறை மறுக்கப்பட்டுப் பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் ஆற்றானாய் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லுவானாய்ச் சொல்லியது தோழி கேட்டுக் குறை முடிப்பது பயன்

thinai_evidence.note: hill farmers' millet and parrots, with a lover's suit refused

210.reading: The friend tells the lord of the rich town, where the seed basket carried to a re-ploughed wet field comes home full of fish, that grand talk and harsh riding are not wealth but the fruit of one's deeds; what the worthy call wealth is the gentle-eyed wealth of a nature that fears the distress of those who depend on one.
210.nuance: The friend grants him entry while lecturing him, and the lecture is a definition of wealth aimed at a rich man who has hurt his dependant wife. The basket that went out with seed and returns with fish (more than was sent) is a near miss for ullurai: one pair only.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகனை நெருங்கிச் சொல்லுவாளாய் வாயில் நேர்ந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: ploughed wet fields and a rich town's lord at fault

211.reading: Alone and overheard, the friend asks to whom she can tell her pain: the lord of the shore, where a bent-backed male prawn that escaped a black-legged heron hunting in the salt pans takes fright at the white screwpine bud on the dune, has abandoned the girl, so they say.
211.nuance: The prawn fears a harmless flower that looks like the heron, as the girl, who has come safely through the lover's absences, now dreads a report (எனவே, so they say) as if it were the desertion itself.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட ஒருதலை ஆற்றாளாம் என்ற தோழி சிறைப்புறமாகத் தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: salt pans, backwater, heron, prawn and screwpine

ullurai.tenor: the girl, afraid of the rumour that the man has left her

pairs.situation: she has come through the dangers of the secret love so far
she now dreads a mere report as though it were the desertion

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a prawn and a screwpine of the shore in a neythal poem (porul 7.27)

212.reading: The friend tells the girl that across the wasteland, where the clear lonely cry of the long-legged kanandhul, afraid of a decoy hunter's net, is caught by passing bards on their strings, and across the tall hills of the Vadugar with their harsh drums and fierce dogs, he has come back to them, who grew anxious each time they heard their little son's sweet voice asking to be held as he looked at the red gold bracelet on his hand.
212.nuance: The bards tune their strings to a frightened bird's cry, so even the road's terror becomes music; the household's anxiety is told through the child, whose request to be held stands for the absent father.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் முடித்துத் தலைமகனோடு வந்த வாயில்கள்வாய் வரவு கேட்ட தோழி தலை மகட்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the wasteland road of the man's journey for wealth

213.reading: Seeking the friend's help, the man asks the long-armed girls which is the small village fenced by great rocks near the roaring falls, where a young red cow eats the ripe jackfruit hanging by the roots of the common's tree where calves are tied and drinks clear water in the bamboo thicket; if they will not say even that, is the guarding of this red-eared millet, swaying after the cloud's rain, theirs too?
213.nuance: The question is a pretext: asking the way and who owns the field is how the lover opens talk, and the second question presses them to admit they are the guards he can meet there.

colophon.thurai: மதி உடன்படுக்கும் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: waterfall, jackfruit and millet field, with the lover approaching the girls

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he addresses the girls in the plural (நீள் தோளீரே)

214.reading: The woman asks her friend whether her lover, who left for wealth saying fame, pleasure and giving do not come to those who sit idle, and who swore he would return to deck her hair with alari flowers, will not hear this rain cloud's voice, flashing as if to mock the grief that loosened her bangles and roaring as if to shout at it.
214.nuance: His reason is a maxim in three terms, quoted back to her, and the season he promised arrives without him: the thunder mocks not his absence but her trust in the maxim and the oath.

colophon.thurai: உலகியலால் பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்ட தலைமகன் குறித்த பருவம் கண்டு தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting as the promised rains come, which is irutthal, not the parting itself

215.reading: As the sun that climbed from the eastern sea sinks behind the western hill and the lonely evening comes, with bangled women lighting fish-fat lamps in the wide houses of the noisy hamlet by the shore, the friend asks the man what harm there is in staying with them tonight, since their kin, out after a shark that tore through their net, have not come back from a failed hunt.
215.nuance: The invitation is also a refusal: staying the night openly in the hamlet is what only a husband could do, so the friend's 'stay' presses for marriage, as the colophon's second reading says.

colophon.thurai: பகற் குறி வந்து மீள்வானை அவள் ஆற்றும் தன்மையள் அல்லள் நீயிர் இங்குத் தங்கற் பாலீர் எமரும் இன்னது ஒரு தவற்றினர் எனத் தோழி தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது இரவுக் குறி மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: sunset in a shore hamlet, the evening sorrow of neythal

occasion.words: இரவுக் குறி மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயதூஉம் ஆம்

216.reading: The other woman, speaking to the bard so the wife's people hear, says that even if her lovers do not come to end her sulking and do not help in her sorrow as the hand helps a hurt eye, the town where they live is not hateful, since one lives where one sees those who look kindly; but others than one's own beloved, even if they are like those who heard of Thirumaavunni, who cut off a breast at the field near the fire-red vengai the god guards, are unbearable.
216.nuance: Thirumaavunni, who tore off a breast when a stranger's trouble wrung her, is a story the poet's audience knew and we only partly know; lines 6 to 11 are hard, and the sense that 'those who heard her story' stand for pitying outsiders is a guess.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகட்குப் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பத் தலைமகன் தலைநின்று ஒழுகப் படாநின்ற பரத்தை பாணற்கு ஆயினும் விறலிக்குஆயினும் சொல்லுவாளாய் நெருங்கிச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the other woman's sulk and the fields of the town

comparisons.tenor: the help a lover should give
the others, who are not her beloved

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: or to the virali; the overhearers are the wife's companions (தலைமகட்குப் பாங்காயினார்)

217.reading: The wife tells her friend that though the man of the hill country, where a fierce elephant, more splendid each time it is seen like the wealth of those who live in fame, takes fright at a tiger and vents its rage on a black-stemmed vengai until its anger cools, is very sweet to her, she will brood and sulk, for making him feel her sulk is the strong way to drive off her long loneliness.
217.nuance: The elephant that fears the tiger and spends its anger on a tree is a near miss for ullurai (the man who takes out on the wife what he dares not face elsewhere): the second pair is not anchored, so it stays scene. Line 9 can also mean that making him understand is hard, which reverses her confidence.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் வாயில் மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulk is marutham's uri, though the things are of the hills (porul 1.15)

comparisons.tenor: the elephant, finer at every sight

218.reading: Answering the friend's reassurance, the girl says the sun has set with dimmed rays, the night grows lonely like a creeper whose flowers have dropped, bats fly to their haunts, the cock calls each time his mate laughs, the season named by the man who swore love on the path has passed, the owl in the forked neem hoots through the night; worn by unending pain, must she still hear alone the andril's cry from the thick palmyra?
218.nuance: Every creature at nightfall either goes home or calls its mate, and the last, the andril, is the bird of inseparable pairs, so the catalogue ends on what she lacks; lines 3 and 4 (the laughing cock) are obscure.

colophon.thurai: வரைவிடை மெலிந்த தலைமகள் வன்புறை எதிர்மொழிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: sunset lament with the andril on the palmyra

219.reading: The girl tells her friend that though her eyes, shoulders and cool fragrant hair lose their old beauty and pallor spreads, and though her life should pass into death, she will not be angry at all, because the lord of the wide shore, where fishermen light flames at night that look like the light of a sun not yet risen, and she joined of their own accord.
219.nuance: தானே யானே: he himself and I myself, with no go-between; the union was their own choice, so there is no one to blame, not even him.

colophon.thurai: வரைவிடை வைத்துப் பிரிய ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: crabs, fishermen and the lord of the shore

220.reading: The little boys who tie small bells to a band, wear erukku-bud garlands, make a horse that does not eat and roam the street with him are truly wise; but the deluded people of this festive town of ever-sounding drums, who call themselves the town, would join him too if they knew fellow-feeling, telling him not to be a stranger to the sweet-voiced girl with eyes like kayal fish.
220.nuance: The boys' game is the madal itself, played as a toy, so the lover's last resort has become a street spectacle children copy; calling the children 'great worthies' (சான்றோர்) mocks the town's elders by contrast.

colophon.thurai: குறை நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளை முகம் புக்கது பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் தோழி கேட்பத் தலைமகளை ஓம்படுத்ததூஉம் ஆம்.தான் ஆற்றானாய்ச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the madal costume and the palm horse, which the Tholkappiyam sets under perunthinai

occasion.words: குறை நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளை முகம் புக்கது

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he speaks to no one named

links.note: Both use the same formula line (செவ் வேர்ப் பலவின் பயம் கெழு கொல்லி) and the god-made image on Kolli that does not decay: in Natrinai 201 the man says the girl stays in his heart like that image under storm and earthquake; in Akananuru 209 the friend says the absent man cannot forget her beauty, which is like that image.
links.teaches: The Kolli image lends its one property, that it does not perish, to the lover's memory in one poem and to the woman's beauty in the other, and both times it answers a doubter (the rebuking companion, the weeping girl), so the image worked as a stock guarantee that a bond will last.

links.note: Both are elopement poems that see the flowering trees of the wasteland as the lamps of a town festival: kongam like Karthigai lamps in Natrinai 202, silk-cotton like a festive town's oil lamps in Akananuru 17.
links.teaches: The eloping man offers the festival-lit forest to the girl as something homely and beautiful, while the foster mother left behind sees the same lights on a waterless road her girl's little feet must cross, so one image of the paalai road comforts or terrifies according to who speaks.

links.note: In both the friend, with the man listening, reads the mother's look at harvest time: in Akananuru 302 the mother keeps the girl home and stares at her body; in Natrinai 206 the father sends her to guard the millet while the mother wishes the wedding vengai would flower and looks at her face.
links.teaches: Together the two show the ripe millet as the moment when the parents read their daughter either as a field guard or as a bride, and the friend in both turns the mother's silent look into the deadline that should make the listening man ask for marriage.

links.note: In Natrinai 208 the friend says the great rain's voice seems to seek out parted lovers and bring them home; in Natrinai 214 the woman hears the rain's voice as flashing and roaring in mockery of her grief, because he has not come.
links.teaches: The monsoon thunder is the same sign of the promised season in both, but the friend before the parting reads it as a power that fetches the man and the wife after the deadline reads it as a jeer, so the rain's meaning in paalai depends on whether the promise is still ahead or already broken.

links.note: Natrinai 210 defines the wealth of the worthy as gentleness that fears the distress of those who depend on one; in Natrinai 214 the man leaves his wife, whose bangles slip from grief, to win wealth because fame, pleasure and giving need it.
links.teaches: By 210's definition the departing man of 214 is pursuing the wrong wealth, since the distress of a dependant is exactly what true wealth fears to cause, so the anthology holds the akam parting for wealth and a moral critique of it side by side.

links.note: Natrinai 210 says grand speech and harsh riding are not wealth, only the fruit of deeds, and the wealth of the worthy is a gentle-eyed nature; Kural 241 says the wealth of grace is the wealth of wealths, since the base also hold goods.
links.teaches: The friend aims the Kural's general ranking of wealths at a particular rich husband who has hurt his wife, and narrows grace to fear of the dependant's distress, so the maxim is shown at work as a rebuke inside a marriage.

links.note: Kural 66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute and lute sweet; in Natrinai 212 the bards tune their strings on the road while at home the child's sweet voice asking to be held made the mother anxious each time.
links.teaches: The child's voice that the Kural ranks above music becomes, while the father is away, a reminder of his absence, so the couplet's household joy assumes the father is present to hear it.

links.note: Kural 613 says the pride of generosity rests on effort; the man of Natrinai 214 leaves saying fame, pleasure and giving do not come to those who sit idle.
links.teaches: The akam poem shows the Kural's rule as a departing husband's stock reason, quoted by the wife he leaves and then mocked by the thunder, so the maxim that giving needs effort was already common speech, and the poem counts what it costs the one left behind.

links.note: Kural 788 says friendship clears distress at once, like the hand of one whose garment slips; the other woman of Natrinai 216 says her lovers do not help her sorrow as the hand helps a hurt eye, yet the town they live in is still sweet.
links.teaches: The parathai admits her lovers fail the Kural's test of friendship, the hand's unthinking help, and still finds their mere presence in town enough, so the pair shows love surviving a failure that by the Kural's measure would end a friendship.

links.note: In Kural 1260 the woman says those whose hearts melt like fat in fire cannot say they will join and then hold out in a sulk; in Natrinai 217 the wife says that though the man is very sweet she will brood and sulk, since making him feel it drives off her loneliness.
links.teaches: The Kural woman doubts that a loving heart can keep a sulk, while the Natrinai wife resolves to keep one precisely because she loves him and wants the long loneliness to end, so the two disagree on whether the sulk is weakness overcome or a strategy of love.

links.note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; in Natrinai 218 the girl, past the promised season, lists the evening's creatures, the bats going home, the cock calling his mate, the owl, and asks if she must hear the andril alone.
links.teaches: The Kural woman makes evening a fellow sufferer, while the Natrinai girl finds every creature of the evening paired or going home, so the same projection onto nightfall can give companionship or prove isolation, and the unmarried girl gets only the second.

links.note: In Kural 1188 the woman says people speak of her pallor but none says he left her; in Natrinai 219 the girl says she will not blame him though pallor spreads and she dies, since he and she joined of their own accord.
links.teaches: The Kural woman complains that blame falls on her skin and not on him, while the Natrinai girl takes the pallor as her own because the union was her own choice, so the pair shows how a self-chosen secret union changes who can be blamed for the suffering.

links.note: Kuruntokai 17 says men whose love hardens ride a palm stem as a horse, wear erukku buds as a garland and become a spectacle in the street; in Natrinai 220 small boys with erukku garlands and a horse that does not eat roam the street with the man.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai 17 states the madal as a lover's desperate public act, and Natrinai 220 shows children copying its very costume as a street game, so the madal was familiar enough to be play, and the lover uses the children's ease against the adults' censure.

links.note: Kural 214 says one who knows what is fitting (ஒப்புரவு) lives and others are counted among the dead; in Natrinai 220 the lover says the townspeople, if they knew ஒப்புரவு, would side with him and tell him not to be a stranger to the girl.
links.teaches: The lover appeals to the Kural's civic duty of fellow-feeling to claim the town's support for a love match it is condemning, so the pair shows ஒப்புரவு invoked against the town's own idea of propriety.

source_issues: 205: line 1 repeats Natrinai 399 line 1 (text flag); a formula opening, not an error.
214: the colophon thinai is பாலை; the poem is a wife waiting as the promised rains arrive (irutthal), so I infer mullai.
217: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி; the things are of the hills but the uri is the wife's sulk and refusal of entry, so I infer marutham, mixed.
220: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி; the poem has no hill things and turns on the madal costume, so I infer perunthinai. The colophon joins two alternatives with a full stop (ஆம்.தான்).
